title: Saint Joan
description: First performed in 1923 and Shaw's greatest tragedy: the trial and execution of Joan of Arc as a conflict between the individual conscience and the institutions of the world. It is a dramatic work of 1923 by George Bernard Shaw; it is catalogued here under Problem Play and Well-Made Drama; Victorian Verse Drama and Revived Tragedy and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Joan, a peasant girl, leads the French armies at Orléans, crowns the Dauphin at Reims, and is then captured, tried by the English and the Inquisition for heresy and executed at Rouen; the epilogue shows her return in a dream to the men who condemned her, and her final refusal to accept a world that cannot bear her.

principal_characters: Joan; Robert de Baudricourt; the Dauphin, later Charles VII; Dunois; the Earl of Warwick; Bishop Cauchon; the Inquisitor; John de Stogumber; La Hire; the Archbishop of Rheims

The author's characteristic manner is extended dialectical argument as dramatic action.

literary_significance: Saint Joan is widely regarded as Shaw's masterpiece and the greatest English history play since Shakespeare: its portrait of Joan as a Protestant before the Reformation and a nationalist before nationalism made the play a landmark of the modern stage, and it won Shaw the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1925.

title: A Book of Nonsense

It is a verse work of 1846 by Edward Lear; it is catalogued here under Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule; Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale.
plot_or_argument: Each page presents a limerick about a person of a place — a man of the hills, a lady of Wales, a young person of Dee — whose odd behaviour or physical peculiarity produces a comic catastrophe, with a drawing that completes the joke and a final line that repeats or echoes the first.

meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The author's characteristic manner is closed stanzaic forms pushed to absurdity.

literary_significance: A Book of Nonsense invented the modern limerick and the modern nonsense book: it established the five-line form, it made nonsense a respectable genre for children, and it was the model for the whole tradition of comic verse from Lear's own later books to the nonsense of the twentieth century.

title: Nonsense Songs, Stories, Botany, and Alphabets

plot_or_argument: The Owl and the Pussy-cat sail away and marry by the light of the moon; the Jumblies go to sea in a sieve and return in triumph; the Duck rides round the world on the Kangaroo's tail, and the Daddy Long-legs and the Fly sail away to the great Gromboolian plain; the botanical plates present absurd plants with mock-scientific names.

title: The Dong with a Luminous Nose
description: Published in Laughable Lyrics (1877) and the most moving of English nonsense poems: the exile's search for the Jumbly Girl he loved. It is a verse work of 1877 by Edward Lear; it is catalogued here under Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule.
plot_or_argument: The Dong, a lonely creature of the shore, falls in love with a Jumbly Girl who sails away with her people; he makes himself a luminous nose of bark and wax to light his way, and wanders the cliffs at night, singing a melancholy song of loss, while the Jumblies dance in the moonlight beyond his reach.
narrative_structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The author's characteristic manner is closed stanzaic forms pushed to absurdity.

title: A Shropshire Lad
description: Published in 1896 at the author's expense and the most popular sequence of English lyrics of its age: poems of the Shropshire countryside, of young men dying and of the brevity of life. It is a verse work of 1896 by A. E. Housman; it belongs to Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet and it is catalogued here under Pastoral Elegy and the Mourning Sequence; Sonnet Revival and Sequenced Sonnet.
plot_or_argument: The sequence moves through the Shropshire landscape from spring to winter: the lad who must leave for London, the soldier who dies in battle, the lovers who are parted, the hanged man and the suicide, all set in a countryside that is beautiful and completely indifferent to the fate of the people in it.
narrative_structure: The work is in 63 poems. An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the ballad and the song measure in quatrains.

The record dates the work as composed between 1895 and 1896 and first published in 1896 and the corpus places it within Victorian High Seriousness and the Public Poet, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; sonnet revival and sequenced sonnet.

It is also the central English text of unavowed homosexuality.

title: Last Poems

title: Peter Pan; or, The Boy Who Would Not Grow Up
description: First performed in 1904 and the most influential children's myth of the modern world: the boy who flies to Never Land and refuses to grow up. It is a dramatic work of 1904 by J. M. Barrie; it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Problem Play and Well-Made Drama.
plot_or_argument: Peter Pan returns to the nursery of the Darling family to find his shadow, takes Wendy and her brothers to Never Land to be his mother, and leads the Lost Boys against Captain Hook and his pirates; Wendy eventually returns home and grows up, while Peter remains a child for ever.
narrative_structure: The action is divided into five acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.

title: The Admirable Crichton

narrative_structure: The action is divided into four acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
principal_characters: Crichton; Lord Loam; Lady Mary Lasenby; Lady Catherine; Lady Agatha; Ernest Woolley; the Reverend John Treherne; Tweeny; Lord Brocklehurst

title: The Little Minister
description: Published in 1891 and the most popular of the Scottish novels: a young minister in a small town falls in love with a mysterious gypsy girl. It is a prose fiction work of 1891 by J. M. Barrie; it is catalogued here under Realist Novel of Common Life; Novel of Development and the Growth Story.
plot_or_argument: Gavin Dishart, the young minister of Thrums, falls in love with Babbie, who roams Thrums disguised as a gypsy girl but is in fact the ward and intended bride of the old Earl of Rintoul; their forbidden love, the town's scandal, and the heroism of the small minister in a riot make a story that mixes kailyard comedy, romance and a glimpse of the Scottish Chartist troubles.

A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.

title: Margaret Ogilvy
description: Published in 1896 and Barrie's memoir of his mother, the book in which the grief that produced Peter Pan is recorded. It is a prose work of 1896 by J. M. Barrie; it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey.

title: Three Men in a Boat (To Say Nothing of the Dog)
description: Published in 1889 and the most durable English comic book of the century: three young men and a dog take a boat up the Thames and fail at everything. It is a prose work of 1889 by Jerome K. Jerome; it is catalogued here under Comic Novel and the New Humour.

title: The Idle Thoughts of an Idle Fellow

title: Maggie: A Girl of the Streets

title: The Red Badge of Courage
